about: The animatic's cut plan, the one file edited by hand: run `tools/assemble.py time` after any change. Voice segments are SCRIPT_V2.md's VOICE paragraphs verbatim; holds are its written silences and beats (and a few added ones, each noted). Shots start at anchors on the voice clock (see tools/assemble.py).
changes: Timing: the cut runs on the scratch narration's measured line lengths (`audio/vo/scratch/lines.json`, 101 lines, each matched to its script paragraph by chapter and number), with a 0.35 s breath between lines and the script's written silences and beats as holds (a beat is 0.8 s). The scratch voice speaks at 157-174 words a minute in chapters 0-6 and 128-137 in chapters 7-9, quicker than the script's plan in the first half, so the film runs 12:09 rather than the script's estimated 12:55. Without a lines.json, `time` falls back to word counts at each chapter's `rate` in `cut.json` (which gave 12:54).

Holds added to the voice clock (all logged in `cut.json` as holds with a note): 1.4 s before the first line (the display settles, "No music for 2 s"); a 0.5 s breath before the cold open's second "Yes." (the direction puts the two YESes 4 s apart) and 0.4 s in chapter 4; 0.8-1.0 s before each chapter's first line so its title can be read (2.6 s in chapter 6, over the locked courtroom); 0.5 s between "2017." and the sentence; 1 s at the end of chapter 3, where the script has none.

The cold open's montage is gfx/montage.py's 6.2 s flash-forward (ten shots, 0.8 s down to 0.5 s each), then the 5 s title: 11.2 s with no voice, against the script's "10 s montage ... 5 s" (ten shots at 0.5-0.8 s cannot fill 10 s).
The chapter titles (gfx/type.html `chapter`) sit on each chapter's first shot and leave before its cut; the cold open has the film title instead.
The flash-forward and the end use the same match cut on the two bags (inspection_room `match` → void_stage `bags`): the push is carried across the cut at the same speed, so the bags stay registered.
problems: Gene is in no plate. Chapter 1's family and all of chapter 8 play on the empty dining room, so the film's planned cut from Gene in his chair to the same chair empty cannot happen; chapter 8 is carried by stand-ins (Tim at the witness table, the Chicago suitcase, the far cell) and is the weakest chapter. Needs: home `dining` with Gene (and Tim) warm for chapter 1, Gene alone in the cold light and in profile in `chair` for chapter 8.

Nothing moves inside the frame: every shot is a still plate with a 2-8 % push. No hand slides the booklet, no head lifts to the tannoy, no one walks; over twelve minutes it reads as a moving slideshow, and the cold open's median shot is 3.0 s against the script's 1.6-2.4 s (the montage's ten cuts aside).

Prison costume continuity: Dawn wears the short-sleeved top at the courtroom dock (06-03, and in the montage) and in the visiting room (07-04, 09-04), while the Void Stage plates have the long-sleeved uniform DECISIONS sets for every prison scene, so the cut alternates between the two outfits.

The tote changes colour between plates: since the 23:13 republish the evidence-table tote is mustard, the inspection-room tote is brown in the split frame (04-10, 04-13) and mustard in `handbags`/`handbags_touch`, and the hotel tote is cognac. The split frame, whose point is "the same tote", shows two different bags.

A small pool of plates, mostly 1280x720: 79 plates over 165 shots, with Dawn standing in the void, Tim at the witness table and the inspection bags each three or four times, and the prison exterior seven times. The 1280 plates are upscaled 1.5x (four framings to 1.18-1.35x more) and look soft beside the 2560 plates (the bags, the purses, the inspection lineup).

Smaller: the Void Stage is 12 % of the running time against 20 %; the emails line on Tim's statement (05-03) is small on a phone; the water glass on Tim's witness desk refracts into what reads as a white figurine; chapter 6's title is up about 2.6 s; the scratch voice is quicker than the script, so the film runs 12:09, not 12:55.

voice.text: The bags are overweight.
Only slightly. There's a small fee, and she pays it without a second thought.
It's 2014, at an airport in China. Dawn Michelle Hunt, an American from Chicago, is checking two bags for the next flight of a trip she won.
Not long after, security staff call her aside. She is led into a room, and her two bags are already there.
The officers want to know one thing. Are these bags hers?
According to her brother, she says yes.
They ask again.

voice.note: added: a held breath before the second Yes (the direction puts the two YESes 4 s apart)

voice.text: Yes.
Why would she say anything else? She packed them herself. She just paid to carry them.
Inside the luggage are designer handbags. And sewn into the linings of those handbags, authorities say, is more than two kilograms of methamphetamine.
Her family says she had no idea it was there. She believed the handbags were a prize, from the people who had paid for the trip of her life.
The luggage was hers. The drugs, she said, were not.
Three years later, a court sentences her to death, with a two-year reprieve. Today, she is serving life.
And twelve years after that airport, her brother appears before American lawmakers with a question that no one in the room can answer.

voice.text: Before China, there was Chicago.
Dawn was a daughter and a sister. A former flight attendant. An artist who loved fashion, and loved to travel.

Her brother Tim remembers her as intelligent, and trusting. She and their mother liked to enter sweepstakes, he told Reuters. For Dawn, every entry was a small possibility that something wonderful might happen.

In 2014 she was working as a receptionist, in a family that had given decades to public service. Her father, Gene, had served in the Army and then as a Chicago police sergeant. Tim had been a Chicago police officer himself.
A family that knew what danger looked like.
What arrived in Dawn's inbox didn't look like danger at all.
It looked like she had won.

The message said she'd won a contest. Accounts differ on exactly what the prize was: cash, travel, or both. But every version has the same shape. An unexpected win, and people ready to fly her across the world.
Dawn didn't believe it. Not at first. Tim says she looked the organizers up online. What she found looked real enough that she sent her passport details.
Then the thing that ended her doubts arrived.
The tickets.
Real tickets to Hong Kong, paid for by someone else.
That is what makes this story so hard to shake. The first part of the promise was true.
Her family believes the deception was hidden in everything that came after.

voice.text: According to Tim's sworn account, Dawn spent nine days in Hong Kong. Sightseeing. Shopping. The people running the trip treated her well, and every expense was covered.
Then they offered more: mainland China. With their help she got a visa, and spent about nine more days travelling through the country.
Watch what those days did.
The email became a ticket. The ticket became a city. And the city became a relationship, with people who had given her nothing but reasons to trust them.
There was more to come. Australia, she was told. Another part of the prize.
For Dawn, the trip of her life was still going.
But before she left China, they had one more gift for her.

voice.text: Just before the next leg of the trip, the organizers told Dawn she had won something else. Designer handbags.
She accepted them. Why wouldn't she? These were the people who had paid for weeks of her life.
But there was a problem. Her luggage was already full.
So, Tim testified, she went with people from the trip to the Baiyun Leather Market, where the organizers bought an extra bag.
Dawn packed the handbags herself. Two pieces of luggage. Both checked in her name.
And at the check-in desk, the scale said what you already know.
Overweight.
She paid the fee.
Tim put that detail in his testimony for a reason. To him, it shows how ordinary this journey felt to his sister.
The people behind the trip had given her the handbags. They had solved her luggage problem. And whatever was hidden in those linings was now travelling in her name.

The trip ended in that room. The case was only beginning.

voice.text: For Dawn, the airport wasn't the end of a bad trip. It was the first day of a detention that would last about three years before any verdict.

Her family says she tried to cooperate. Tim testified that she answered investigators' questions, and gave them the emails she had received from the organizers. The same emails that had started it all.
It wasn't enough.

Her family also alleges something worse. In testimony to Congress in 2024, Tim said Dawn had told their father she was sexually assaulted in the detention facility. That allegation has not been independently established in the sources available to us.
We are not going to recreate it. It is serious enough to state plainly, and Dawn has already lost control of so much of her own story.
For three years, her family waited for a trial to correct what they believed was a terrible mistake.
The verdict was worse than anything they had feared.

voice.text: A death sentence, with a two-year reprieve.
The words matter. It was not an order for her immediate execution. It was a suspended death sentence, and it was later reduced to life in prison.

China sees the case as closed. Asked about it in 2026, China's foreign ministry told Reuters that Dawn and another imprisoned American were serving sentences for serious drug-related crimes, and that their legal rights and health were being protected.
Her family sees a scam victim. They insist she was what investigators call a blind mule: someone who carries drugs for traffickers without knowing it.

And this is the part they find hardest to accept. According to her family, and to reporting on the court's reasoning, the judge recognised that Dawn had been deceived, and concluded that she should have known anyway.
Deceived.
And guilty anyway.

voice.text: Dawn is held at Guangdong Women's Prison. It's where her brother has gone to visit her.

In 2024, Tim told Congress that his sister had lost weight, and become pale. Prison doctors had found uterine fibroids, and raised the possibility of ovarian cancer. A possibility, not a diagnosis. She'd had heavy bleeding, and blood transfusions. Doctors recommended a hysterectomy. She refused, Tim said, in part because she did not trust the people responsible for her care.

At home in Chicago, the family turned the case into a campaign. Tim wrote to officials and to lawyers. In September 2024, he testified before a congressional commission, and his sister's case became part of the public record.

In May 2025, according to Tim, the United States formally requested her release on humanitarian grounds. Members of Congress introduced a bipartisan bill carrying her name, and the name of another American imprisoned in China, Nelson Wells Junior.
Every letter, every hearing, every request was a door that might open.
None of them brought her home.
And the man who had waited longest was running out of time.

voice.text: Six months later, in July 2026, Tim went back to the prison.
He told lawmakers he barely recognised his sister. She seemed frail. Stooped. Her teeth had changed. Her hair was much greyer than two years before. She struggled to focus on their conversation.
But there was one thing she kept coming back to.
One question.
When would she be released?
Tim could not give her a date.
In September 2026, he appeared before Congress again. There was no reunion to report. Only an empty place at the family table, and a brother still fighting.
Remember the question at the beginning of this story? The one no one in that room could answer.
It was never really his question.
It was hers.
As of November 2026, Dawn Michelle Hunt is still in prison in China. Her family is still asking for her release on humanitarian grounds.
The State Department's advice is simple: never carry gifts or luggage across a border for people you do not truly know. Dawn thought she knew them. She had spent weeks in their company.
Twelve years ago, in a room at an airport, officers asked her a question. She answered it. Yes.
Now she is the one asking.
